paragraphs.text: Muyun Da Hong Pao is a [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition), the oolong of the Wuyi Mountains in northern Fujian, where the bushes grow among rock on ledges and terraces in cliff country. The name [Da Hong Pao](yancha:da-hong-pao), Big Red Robe, began with six mother trees on a cliff at Jiulongke, and picking from them stopped in 2006. What is sold under the name today is tea from Qidan, the cultivar grown from cuttings of those trees, or more often a blend of several Wuyi cultivars.

This leaf was twisted into long strips and given a heavy roast over charcoal, the way Wuyi tea is finished: in [several rounds](yancha:making) with rests of weeks or months between them, not in one pass. The roast dries the tea so it keeps, and the maker matches its strength to the leaf.

The label names the Wuyi Mountains without a zone or a pit, so it does not say how close to the [true rock core](wuyi-mountains:zones) the bushes grew. The trade sorts Wuyi tea by that distance, from the stony core out through the half rock ring to the river banks.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
